utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military-style uniform with a camouflage pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there -- and what colour was this uniform?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather dark green dappled with a -- as I said -- and it has a camouflage pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in what condition was this person -- were these two young Serbs that you saw in the basement?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Before that I would like to add something to finish what I began to describe. When we went to the basement, they were in a rather poor condition. But according to the words of Maxhup and a local soldier, the name of one of them was either Senad or Nenad, but I think it was Senad, and that he was a police officer, the one wearing the uniform. I think that was his name. I may be mistaken. I'm not certain now whether the name was Senad or Nenad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say they were in a rather poor condition, could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty badly beaten up with bruises, dirty, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in this basement other than these two Serbs that you've -- two young Serbs that you've described?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, there was me and one of my companions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I meant were there any other prisoners in the basement other than these two Serbs that you've described?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. I didn't understand. Apart from these two there were a couple of older people, mostly men, but also some women.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know -- when you say "a couple of older people, mostly men, but also women," how many people approximately are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I didn't count them. I didn't go there to count and inspect the conditions. I was there on a different mission. How should I describe it? I was there to carry some mail. And during the conversation he told me, "I caught two young Serbs," and then I went to see them. But how many of them there were inside I really wouldn't -- couldn't say. It wasn't a big room like this courtroom we're in now and I didn't pay so much attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But when you say that there was a group of people there, are you talking about 20 or 30, more than that, less than that? Can you give us -- can you just try to give us an estimate of how many people you think you saw there? And, sir, before you answer, just as I had explained before, you have to wait until I turn off the microphone. You can go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately nine or ten, but I really didn't count so I couldn't give you an exact number. It wasn't a large room. It was just a -- just an ordinary basement of a house, maybe 4 metres by 4, not a large hall. So I would -- it was a room that didn't hold very many people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you went there the first time you told us that you saw that there was water in this basement. On this second occasion when you went down to the basement, did you also see water there?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention, as I told you. I didn't really look for water. I can only tell you what I remember. I saw some blood-stains on the walls. So whatever caught my eye I can tell you, but whether there was water the second time or the third time, I really don't remember. Once I entered this -- the other time I didn't enter at all and the third time I entered again, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us there were women there. Do you recall approximately how many women were being held in this basement? Just roughly, to the best of your recollection, sir.

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that there were a couple of women, but again I didn't count. I'm sorry. There were around nine or ten persons in all. Certainly there were fewer women than men. The ratio may have been three to six, but I didn't pay attention really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've told us that two of these persons held in the basement were Serb. Can you help us with the ethnicity of the other persons who you saw there?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot because I didn't ask them what ethnicity they were. I didn't have the right to, so I really can't help you there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to find out that two of these persons were Serb, two of the persons that you saw there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that when we said hello that Maxhup said that he had captured two young Serbs. I knew then that they were Serbs and, of course, by their uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Maxhup or anyone else there tell you anything about how these two Serbs had been captured?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that they took them prisoner. If I remember correctly, they were captured in a car, they were in a car together, or so I was told. Yes, I think they were captured in a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've told us that one of these two Serb men was in a uniform. Was anyone else of the persons you saw in this basement dressed in a uniform or wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from him, no, from what I could see at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you do after you visited this basement and saw these people there?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went back upstairs, and when I say "upstairs," I mean the office or at least the room that they used as an office. We finished our business there and went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "we finished our business there," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we delivered to them something that they needed. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what it was that you delivered on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. It was in a bag and -- a handbag and I didn't look in to see what was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, during this third visit, did you see any one of these persons who were held in that basement being interrogated or questioned by any of the KLA soldiers that were there?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot. I'm sorry. There's one other thing I have to tell you, to just finish the story. When we went upstairs to the office, and I said it was to the right as you entered the front door, it was the second office on the right-hand side, and there -- Maxhup asked the local policeman -- the local soldier to bring over the man in uniform, and that was where the interrogation started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you present during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes -- well, a couple of minutes I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened during this interrogation of the man in uniform?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interrogation was the same as the one I described to you before, where the location of the check-point was, where the police was located, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this person, the man in uniform who was questioned in this office on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that his name was Senad or Nenad, though probably the latter. I may be mistaken, but that's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who did the questioning during this interrogation of this individual?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who else but Maxhup? He was there for that sort of thing so, of course, it would be him conducting the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present in the room other than Maxhup and yourself?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, Maxhup was there, a local soldier of his, and of course my comrade, the one who always accompanied me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why were you there in that room for that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there because I happened to be there. As I told you, I went upstairs from the basement and that room to finish off the business that we had, and in the meantime they brought the man over and we just lingered there a bit. We were freshmen in that sort of business, so we just wanted to stay on and see how this sort of thing is done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "this sort of thing is done," what are you referring to? You said you wanted to see how this sort of thing is done, what are you referring to by "this sort of thing"?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How one is interrogated, because this was the first time that there was someone in a uniform belonging to the enemy side. So I was interested in seeing how an enemy is questioned and how an enemy is made to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how was this person questioned and made to speak?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as the situations we described previously, of course no enemy is willing to tell you and give you information right away, and Maxhup was known to be wielding a baseball bat and was known that -- for beating people up, knocking nine balls out of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. But what I'm asking you is: How was this person in uniform whom you think was called Senad or Nenad questioned by Maxhup on that occasion? Can you just tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just did. Maxhup is known for wielding a baseball bat. Of course he didn't offer him a coffee and tell him to take a seat. He was beating him up, asking about his fellow soldiers, the check-point, et cetera. And of course he was telling him, "Tell me where your fellow soldiers are and then we can make a deal," but of course they were not fellow soldiers, they were the enemy. So he was using his baseball bat for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that Maxhup was beating him up. Where was Maxhup hitting him, I mean in which part of the body was he hitting him?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over his body. I can't single out any specific body part such as head or anything. He was hitting him all over the body, and I didn't really pay specific attention to where the bat would land. But he would hit him all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during this beating, did this person who was being interrogated say anything?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was pleading for his life, weeping, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say that he was pleading for his life, what exactly did you hear him say?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "Don't kill me. I've done nothing wrong," that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did anyone else participate in this beating, other than Maxhup?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, no. Halfway through the beating we went, we had to get back. And for as long as I was there, from what I recall there wasn't anybody else involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there anyone recording the answers this person was giving during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an odd question you're asking me. I didn't pay attention to that, but, of course, in any military setting if there is anything to make a note of, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did this beating take place?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't keep count of the time. It didn't last that long, 15 to 20 minutes perhaps, approximately. As I told you, after that first beating we left, we had to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you later -- you said you had to go back. Did you later return to Jabllanice village?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not again, and let me explain why. Several months later, a major offensive was launched by the Serb forces and we all withdrew. We all withdrew from the points where we were. The offensive was so fierce that we weren't able to defend ourselves against it, and I never went back there again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to go back to this interrogation that you witnessed. Could you describe this person to us, the person in uniform, who was being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was as tall as me, perhaps a bit taller. His hair was blond and he was gaunt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Maxhup or anyone else, any other of the soldiers there, tell you anything about how long this person had been detained in this basement in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never asked him and he never told us how long he was there. As a soldier you are not entitled to put questions to anyone. I wasn't there to ask about what was going on. I was there to do the job I was given and it wasn't up to me to be asking about the man or how long he had been there. I apologise, but that was the case. So he never told me anything and I never asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you told us when you arrived there Maxhup had told you that he had captured two Serbs. Did he mention anything about how many days had gone by since he had captured these individuals?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Truly I apologise, but I don't remember. The only thing I know is that he told us that he was captured, but I don't recall him saying when or where.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this other -- the other prisoners you saw in that basement?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We went back to our zone, so I really don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what about this person whose interrogation you witnessed, do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what became of him. I suppose he, being an enemy and having a uniform, did not meet a good end, but I don't know what happened. I explained to you we left for our zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you've told us that this person was in uniform. Do you know which force he belonged to? And I'm not asking the specific unit, but do you know which force he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what specific unit that was. It was an enemy unit. I know that it was a Serbian unit, but which unit, what it was, I don't know. I only know that he was an enemy to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not asking which unit specifically he belonged to, but do you know which force he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that after this occasion you went back to your zone and that you didn't return later, is that correct, that you didn't return on an additional occasion to Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At any time during these visits you made there, were you able to obtain any information as to why persons were being held in the basement of this house in Jabllanice that you visited?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course, because they weren't members of our ethnicity, that's to say Albanians, they were either Serbs, the Roma, or the Catholics. Let me explain one thing to you. All those who failed to co-operate who did not wear a uniform were either disabled or were not Albanians or were collaborators of the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say all of those who failed to co-operate, what do you mean exactly, failed to co-operate with whom?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but you asked me what I thought happened in that house. So I'm telling you about this specific event. Kosovo is a large place. I can't refer to the general situation. So I'm referring to that person in the house who didn't have a uniform, and it -- you can tell easily who he was. He was either a spy, pardon my expression, but he wouldn't co-operate or he was of a different religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that answer, sir. You're saying you're referring to that person in the house who didn't have a uniform. Are you speaking about a particular individual or are you just generally speaking about persons without uniforms? It's not clear to me from your answer.

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make this quite clear, I'm talking about the house where we were and I cannot speak for the village. There were villagers there, so I can't say that every one of them who didn't have a uniform was either a spy or refused to co-operate. I'm speaking about the situation where I was present, i.e., in that specific house. I can't say everyone because there was an entire village there. Imagine me saying that all of them were this and that. It's impossible. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir, you're speaking about the house which we've been discussing in your testimony, the house with the basement. I'm just trying to understand whom you're referring to when you say that they were either spies or refused to co-operate.

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean those who were in the basement. So let me explain this once again. When I say those who did not wear a uniform, I mean the persons who were present in that basement, either on the first or the second or the third occasion. I am referring to the individuals who were there, not the houses in general but those specific houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why do you say, sir, that those persons who were held in the basement that you saw were either persons who were spies or had refused to co-operate? What is your basis to say that?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the fact that had he been an ordinary villager, he would not have had his hands tied and kept in that basement or be beaten up, and it's on that basis that I would characterise the person as either of the two things, a spy or not of our religion. Otherwise, what would that person be doing in that basement, tied up, and beaten blue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know why it is, sir, that persons were held in this house -- in the basement of this house in Jabllanice village? Why did this --

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't finished my question. Do you know why this house with the basement where people were held existed in Jabllanice village?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an easy thing to find out. The village of Jabllanice is a bit further away from the main road where there was a presence of the Serb units and paramilitary units. It's in a location that is a bit remote, and that's why it was better suited than some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Sir, you told us that you saw Ramush Haradinaj on the first occasion that you went to Jabllanice. Did you see him there on any of the other occasions that you visited the village of Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. Because two or three days before, Mr. Ramush Haradinaj became the commander for the overall Dukagjini area and I was small fry and couldn't expect to see him. It would have been a great honour to meet him at the time, but I never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "two or three days before," before when? When exactly are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was April or May of 1998 that all of this happened, that he became the commander in charge based on his courage and numerous successes in combat. It was on that basis that he became Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir. But when you said "two or three days before," are you referring to some period before one of your visits or were you referring to another time-period?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, before the second incident. Let's make this clear. Before the second visit, my second visit to the village of Jabllanice, that was the time I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us during your first trip there you saw Mr. Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger. Did you see him at this house in Jabllanice on any of the other two occasions that you visited?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again. I saw him that once when he came and never again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've told us also -- you referred to a person by the name of Idriz Gashi and you mentioned that you saw him there on the first occasion. Did you see him on any of the other occasions that you visited the village of Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him. Since he was of that village I saw him the next time as well. He was a local soldier, so of course I met him the second and the third time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have also referred to a person by the name of Nazmi Brahimaj and you said you met him there when you went there for the first time -- when you went to Jabllanice for the first time. Did you see Nazmi Brahimaj on any of the other two occasions that you visited Jabllanice village?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once more. I don't know if it was on the second or the third occasion, but when Ramush Haradinaj became the Commander-in-Chief for the overall zone, unless I'm mistaken, if I remember correctly, Nazmi Brahimaj became the commander of the Jabllanice Zone. It's not as large as the Dukagjini Zone. But at any rate, at that point he became the commander of the Jabllanice Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told me earlier today when I asked you who was the commander of this house with the basement where people were held, you told me that you thought it was Lahi Brahimaj. After Nazmi Brahimaj became the commander of the zone, do you know if Lahi Brahimaj remained the person in charge of this house where persons were held in Jabllanice or did someone else become in charge of that? If you know.

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying "commander." There was commanders commanding at various levels, squad, platoon, company, and so on, in accordance with the hierarchy of the army. But the commander of the unit that was in charge of that house was Maxhup clearly. The commander of the village - and I mean Jabllanice - was his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say the commander of the village was his brother, can you just be clear as to the name of the brother?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nazmi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say he was the commander of the village, are you referring to the period you've just mentioned when you said he became the commander of Jabllanice zone or are you referring to a period before that?

utterances.speaker: 81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same period as I said. After the first time I had gone there, that is, two or three days before going there for the second time and that was two or three weeks after the first visit, Ramush Haradinaj had become the commander of the whole zone. At that moment, Nazmi Brahimaj became village commander. Why? If you want to know I can tell you that I had the honour to meet both of them. Nazmi Brahimaj is an honourable man who was frank to me and sincere to me, and he told me about it. But I don't want to comment any further because he is really very strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Kravetz. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. As Your Honour knows, there are certain issues outstanding. I don't know if you want me to address you on it. I was going to invite you to adjourn until tomorrow afternoon. If you would like me to address you on it, then I would like to do so in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you address us tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you do it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm hoping that the issues will be resolved by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. You -- or you were asking for an adjournment now. Okay. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. We stand adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
